claims.evidence: This is based on behavioral comprehension data and shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: There is no evidence for a potential difference in comprehension, attention or motivation between early blind and sighted groups.
claims.source: The lack of effect for the factor blindness suggests that there is no evidence for a potential difference in comprehension, attention or motivation between groups.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the non-significant effect of blindness on behavioral performance.

claims.claim: The overall coherence spectrum between the amplitude envelope of speech and the MEG signal was maximal over temporal sensors between 6 Hz and 7 Hz.
claims.source: The overall coherence spectrum, which highlights the relationship between the amplitude envelope of speech and the signal recorded from the brain, was maximal over temporal sensors between 6 Hz and 7 Hz (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is based on MEG coherence analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The peak coherence frequency in the current study is slightly higher than those reported in previous studies.
claims.source: The peak in the current study is slightly higher than those reported in previous studies (Gross et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature cited.

claims.claim: The difference in syllabic rate between English (~6.2 Hz) and Italian (~7 Hz) likely explains the shift in peak coherence frequency.
claims.source: A likely explanation for this shift is the difference in syllabic rate between English (~6.2 Hz), used in previous studies, and Italian (~7 Hz) (Pellegrino et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known syllabic rates and citation to Pellegrino et al. (2011).

claims.claim: The syllabic rate is the main carrier of amplitude fluctuations in speech.
claims.source: The syllabic rate is the main carrier of amplitude fluctuations in speech, and thus is most prone to reset oscillatory activity.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about speech processing.

claims.claim: Source-reconstructed coherence was strongest across groups and conditions in bilateral temporal lobes, including primary auditory cortex.
claims.source: The source-reconstructed coherence at the frequency-range of interest confirmed that cerebro-acoustic coherence was strongest across groups and conditions in bilateral temporal lobes, including primary auditory cortex. (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is based on source reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Synchronization to the envelope of speech was stronger in right superior and middle temporal cortex when participants had access to the content of the story.
claims.source: The resulting statistical map (Figure 1G, p<0.05, FWE-corrected) revealed a cluster in right superior and middle temporal cortex (STG, MTG), where synchronization to the envelope of speech was stronger when participants had access to the content of the story.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing intelligible versus non-intelligible conditions, shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The effect of intelligibility on the sensory response suggests an interface between acoustic speech processing and comprehension in STG that is present in both groups.
claims.source: In other words, the effect of intelligibility on the sensory response (coherence with the speech envelope) suggests an interface between acoustic speech processing and comprehension in STG that is present in both groups.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing intelligibility effects in STG.

claims.claim: Enhanced coherence in early blind versus sighted individuals was observed in parieto-occipital cortex along the medial wall, centered on bilateral Precuneus.
claims.source: The statistical maps (Figure 1H, p<0.05, FWE-corrected) revealed enhanced coherence in EB versus SI in parieto-occipital cortex along the medial wall, centered on bilateral Precuneus, branching more extensively into the right hemisphere (see Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing EB and SI groups, shown in Figure 1H and Table 2.

claims.claim: Neuronal populations in blind parieto-occipital cortex show enhanced synchronization to the acoustic speech signal.
claims.source: This main effect of group highlights that neuronal populations in blind parieto-occipital cortex show enhanced synchronization to the acoustic speech signal.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the group difference in coherence.

claims.claim: Blind participants show a stronger sensitivity to the sensory properties of the external speech stimulus in parieto-occipital cortex.
claims.source: That is, blind participants show a stronger sensitivity to the sensory properties of the external speech stimulus at this level.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the enhanced coherence in EB.

claims.claim: A significant effect of the interaction between blindness and intelligibility was observed in right calcarine sulcus.
claims.source: A significant effect of the interaction between blindness and intelligibility [(natEB – 1-channelEB) – (natSI – 1-channelSI)] was observed in right calcarine sulcus.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the interaction effect.

claims.claim: Intelligible speech selectively engages the area around the right calcarine sulcus in the blind versus the sighted.
claims.source: This shows that intelligible speech selectively engages the area around the right calcarine sulcus in the blind versus the sighted.
claims.evidence: This is based on the interaction analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: The region corresponding to right 'visual' cortex showed enhanced sensitivity to intelligible speech in early blind versus sighted individuals.
claims.source: Specifically, the region corresponding to right 'visual' cortex showed enhanced sensitivity to intelligible speech in EB versus SI (p<0.05, FWE-corrected).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the interaction effect.

claims.claim: The analysis contrasting the two intelligible conditions (natural and 8-channel) did not yield a significant effect in the early blind.
claims.source: However, the analysis contrasting the two intelligible conditions (nat and 8-channel) did not yield a significant effect in the EB, suggesting that the low-level degrading of the stimulus alone does not drive the effect, but rather the intelligibility of the speech segment.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing the two intelligible conditions.

claims.claim: Low-level degrading of the stimulus alone does not drive the effect in calcarine sulcus, but rather the intelligibility of the speech segment.
claims.source: However, the analysis contrasting the two intelligible conditions (nat and 8-channel) did not yield a significant effect in the EB, suggesting that the low-level degrading of the stimulus alone does not drive the effect, but rather the intelligibility of the speech segment.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference between natural and 8-channel conditions.

claims.claim: Coherence was stronger during the intelligible condition for early blind versus sighted individuals.
claims.source: Follow-up post hoc comparisons between the two groups revealed that coherence was stronger during the intelligible condition for EB versus SI (t[30] = 3.09, p=0.004), but not during the unintelligible condition (t[30] = –1.08, p=0.29).
claims.evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical comparisons.

claims.claim: Coherence during the unintelligible condition did not differ between early blind and sighted individuals.
claims.source: Follow-up post hoc comparisons between the two groups revealed that coherence was stronger during the intelligible condition for EB versus SI (t[30] = 3.09, p=0.004), but not during the unintelligible condition (t[30] = –1.08, p=0.29).
claims.evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical comparisons.

claims.claim: A group difference between early blind and sighted individuals across conditions was not observed in the calcarine region.
claims.source: A group difference between EB and SI across conditions was not observed in the calcarine region (t[30] = 1.1, p=0.28).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison.

claims.claim: The lack of an overall group effect in calcarine sulcus suggests that there is not a simple enhanced sensory response to speech in the blind.
claims.source: The lack of an overall group effect in calcarine sulcus suggests that there is not a simple enhanced sensory response to speech in the blind.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of main effect of group in calcarine sulcus.

claims.claim: The response in calcarine sulcus only differed between the two groups when speech was intelligible.
claims.source: Rather, the response in calcarine sulcus only differed between the two groups when speech was intelligible.
claims.evidence: This is based on the interaction effect and post-hoc comparisons.

claims.claim: Overall coherence with the speech envelope was equally high in early blind and sighted individuals.
claims.source: While overall coherence with the speech envelope was equally high in EB and SI, the blind population showed significantly higher coherence in the intelligible speech condition than did the sighted, who showed higher cerebro-acoustic coherence in the unintelligible condition (1-Chan).
claims.evidence: This is based on the pattern of results from the interaction analysis.

claims.claim: The blind population showed significantly higher coherence in the intelligible speech condition than did the sighted.
claims.source: While overall coherence with the speech envelope was equally high in EB and SI, the blind population showed significantly higher coherence in the intelligible speech condition than did the sighted, who showed higher cerebro-acoustic coherence in the unintelligible condition (1-Chan).
claims.evidence: This is based on post-hoc comparisons.

claims.claim: Sighted individuals showed higher cerebro-acoustic coherence in the unintelligible condition.
claims.source: While overall coherence with the speech envelope was equally high in EB and SI, the blind population showed significantly higher coherence in the intelligible speech condition than did the sighted, who showed higher cerebro-acoustic coherence in the unintelligible condition (1-Chan).
claims.evidence: This is based on the pattern of results from the interaction analysis.

claims.claim: The more adverse the listening condition, the more the visual cortex is entrained to the visual speech signal when presented together with varying levels of acoustic noise.
claims.source: The latter is reminiscent of the fact that the more adverse the listening condition (low signal-to-noise ratio or audiovisual incongruence), the more the visual cortex is entrained to the visual speech signal of actual acoustic speech when presented together with varying levels of acoustic noise (Park et al., 2016; Giordano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Park et al. (2016) and Giordano et al. (2017).

claims.claim: Giordano et al. (2017) showed an increase of directed connectivity between superior frontal regions and visual cortex under the most challenging conditions.
claims.source: Moreover, Giordano et al. (2017) showed an increase of directed connectivity between superior frontal regions and visual cortex under the most challenging (acoustic noise and uninformative visual cues) conditions, again suggesting a link between the reorganization observed in the occipital cortex of blind individuals and typical multisensory pathways involving the occipital cortex in audio-visual speech processing (Kayser et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Giordano et al. (2017).

claims.claim: Visual deprivation since birth triggers a functional reorganization of the calcarine region that can dynamically interact with the intelligibility of the speech signal.
claims.source: Visual deprivation since birth, however, triggers a functional reorganization of the calcarine region that can then dynamically interact with the intelligibility of the speech signal.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings showing intelligibility-dependent responses in calcarine sulcus of EB.

claims.claim: A main effect was observed only for blindness on functional connectivity between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus.
claims.source: A main effect was observed only for blindness (χ[1] = 4.32, p=0.038) and was caused by greater connectivity for EB versus SI (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis of phase-locking values.

claims.claim: Greater connectivity between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus was observed for early blind versus sighted individuals.
claims.source: A main effect was observed only for blindness (χ[1] = 4.32, p=0.038) and was caused by greater connectivity for EB versus SI (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: The main effects of intelligibility and of the interaction between intelligibility and blindness on functional connectivity were non-significant.
claims.source: The main effects of intelligibility and of the interaction between intelligibility and blindness were non-significant (p=0.241 and p=0.716, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis.

claims.claim: Only the main effect of blindness was significant on the directional information flow between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus.
claims.source: Here, only the main effect of blindness was significant (χ[1] = 4.54, p=0.033), indicating that the directional information flow differs between groups.
claims.evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis of phase-slope index.

claims.claim: The directional information flow between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus differs between early blind and sighted groups.
claims.source: Here, only the main effect of blindness was significant (χ[1] = 4.54, p=0.033), indicating that the directional information flow differs between groups.
claims.evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis of phase-slope index.

claims.claim: The effect of intelligibility on directional information flow was non-significant.
claims.source: The effect of intelligibility and the interaction between intelligibility and blindness were both non-significant (p=0.51 and p=0.377, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis.

claims.claim: The interaction between intelligibility and blindness on directional information flow was non-significant.
claims.source: The effect of intelligibility and the interaction between intelligibility and blindness were both non-significant (p=0.51 and p=0.377, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis.

claims.claim: Sighted individuals showed a significant direction bias from calcarine sulcus to superior temporal gyrus.
claims.source: Follow-up post-hoc one-sample t-tests on the phase slope estimates for each group individually revealed a significant direction bias from CS to STG for SI (t[14] = –2.22, p=0.044).
claims.evidence: This is based on post-hoc one-sample t-tests on phase-slope index.

claims.claim: No directional bias was found for early blind individuals.
claims.source: No directional bias was found for EB (t[16] = 0.74, p=0.47).
claims.evidence: This is based on post-hoc one-sample t-tests on phase-slope index.

claims.claim: Calcarine sulcus projects predominantly to superior temporal gyrus in sighted individuals.
claims.source: As depicted in Figure 2C–D, these results suggest that CS projects predominantly to STG in SI, whereas in EB, this interaction is more balanced and trending in the opposite direction.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phase-slope index results shown in Figure 2C-D.

claims.claim: In early blind individuals, the interaction between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus is more balanced and trending in the opposite direction compared to sighted individuals.
claims.source: As depicted in Figure 2C–D, these results suggest that CS projects predominantly to STG in SI, whereas in EB, this interaction is more balanced and trending in the opposite direction.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phase-slope index results shown in Figure 2C-D.

claims.claim: The region around the Precuneus/Cuneus area is involved in low-level processing of acoustic information alone.
claims.source: That is, the region around the Precuneus/Cuneus area seems to be involved in low-level processing of acoustic information alone.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the finding that this region shows enhanced synchronization irrespective of intelligibility.

claims.claim: The Precuneus/Cuneus area enhances its response to auditory information after early, but not late, visual deprivation.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated that this area enhances its response to auditory information after early, but not late, visual deprivation (Collignon et al., 2013) and maintains this elevated response to sound even after sight-restoration early in life (Collignon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Collignon et al. (2013) and Collignon et al. (2015).

claims.claim: The Precuneus/Cuneus area maintains elevated response to sound even after sight-restoration early in life.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated that this area enhances its response to auditory information after early, but not late, visual deprivation (Collignon et al., 2013) and maintains this elevated response to sound even after sight-restoration early in life (Collignon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Collignon et al. (2015).

claims.claim: Previous studies did not find that the Precuneus/Cuneus area's crossmodal response was related to a specific cognitive function, but rather pointed to a more general response to sounds.
claims.source: These studies did not find that this crossmodal response was related to a specific cognitive function, but rather pointed to a more general response to sounds (Collignon et al., 2013, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Collignon et al. (2013, 2015).

claims.claim: The Precuneus/Cuneus area is capable of parsing complex temporal patterns in sounds but is insensitive to the intelligibility of speech.
claims.source: Interestingly, the current data suggest that this area is capable of parsing complex temporal patterns in sounds but is insensitive to the intelligibility of speech, again suggesting a more general role in sound processing.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the current study's findings showing enhanced synchronization irrespective of intelligibility.

claims.claim: The pattern of local encoding in early blind individuals was accompanied by enhanced occipito-temporal connectivity during speech comprehension as compared to sighted individuals.
claims.source: This pattern of local encoding was accompanied by enhanced occipito-temporal connectivity during speech comprehension in EB as compared to SI.
claims.evidence: This is based on the connectivity analysis results.

claims.claim: Sighted individuals show the expected feed-forward projections from occipital to temporal regions.
claims.source: SI show the expected feed-forward projections from occipital to temporal regions (Lamme et al., 1998), whereas EB show a more balanced connectivity profile, trending towards the reverse temporal to occipital direction (see Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on phase-slope index analysis and citation to Lamme et al. (1998).

claims.claim: Early blind individuals show a more balanced connectivity profile between occipital and temporal regions, trending towards the reverse temporal to occipital direction.
claims.source: SI show the expected feed-forward projections from occipital to temporal regions (Lamme et al., 1998), whereas EB show a more balanced connectivity profile, trending towards the reverse temporal to occipital direction (see Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on phase-slope index analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The findings support the idea of a reverse hierarchical model of the occipital cortex in early blind individuals.
claims.source: These findings support the idea of a reverse hierarchical model (Büchel, 2003) of the occipital cortex in EB, where the regions typically coding for 'low-level' visual features in the sighted (e.g. visual contrast or orientation) participate in higher-level function (e.g. speech intelligibility).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to Büchel (2003).

claims.claim: In a reverse hierarchical model, regions typically coding for 'low-level' visual features in the sighted participate in higher-level function in early blind individuals.
claims.source: These findings support the idea of a reverse hierarchical model (Büchel, 2003) of the occipital cortex in EB, where the regions typically coding for 'low-level' visual features in the sighted (e.g. visual contrast or orientation) participate in higher-level function (e.g. speech intelligibility).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to Büchel (2003).

claims.claim: Previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of early blind people during Braille reading.
claims.source: Indeed, previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of EB people during Braille reading (Sadato et al., 1996; Burton et al., 2002, 2012), verbal memory and verb generation tasks (Amedi et al., 2003), and during auditory language-related processing (Bedny et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of early blind people during verbal memory and verb generation tasks.
claims.source: Indeed, previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of EB people during Braille reading (Sadato et al., 1996; Burton et al., 2002, 2012), verbal memory and verb generation tasks (Amedi et al., 2003), and during auditory language-related processing (Bedny et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Amedi et al. (2003).

claims.claim: Previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of early blind people during auditory language-related processing.
claims.source: Indeed, previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of EB people during Braille reading (Sadato et al., 1996; Burton et al., 2002, 2012), verbal memory and verb generation tasks (Amedi et al., 2003), and during auditory language-related processing (Bedny et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bedny et al. (2011).

claims.claim: Activity in primary occipital regions in early blind people is stronger in a semantic versus a phonologic task.
claims.source: In line with our results, activity in primary occipital regions in EB people is stronger in a semantic versus a phonologic task (Burton et al., 2003), and vary as a function of syntactic and semantic complexity (Röder et al., 2002; Bedny et al., 2011; Lane et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burton et al. (2003).

claims.claim: Activity in primary occipital regions in early blind people varies as a function of syntactic and semantic complexity.
claims.source: In line with our results, activity in primary occipital regions in EB people is stronger in a semantic versus a phonologic task (Burton et al., 2003), and vary as a function of syntactic and semantic complexity (Röder et al., 2002; Bedny et al., 2011; Lane et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Röder et al. (2002), Bedny et al. (2011), and Lane et al. (2015).

claims.claim: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation over the occipital pole induces more semantic errors than phonologic errors in a verb-generation task in early blind people.
claims.source: Moreover, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the occipital pole induces more semantic errors than phonologic errors in a verb-generation task in EB people (Amedi et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Amedi et al. (2003).

claims.claim: The results clearly suggest that the involvement of the occipital pole for language is not fully abstracted from sensory inputs.
claims.source: As we show that occipital regions entrain to the envelope of speech and are enhanced by its intelligibility, our results clearly suggest that the involvement of the occipital pole for language is not fully abstracted from sensory inputs as previously suggested (Bedny, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in contrast to previous suggestions.

claims.claim: The role of the occipital cortex in tracking the flow of speech in early blind people may constitute an adaptive strategy to boost perceptual sensitivity at informational peaks in language.
claims.source: The role of the occipital cortex in tracking the flow of speech in EB people may constitute an adaptive strategy to boost perceptual sensitivity at informational peaks in language.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claims.claim: Language is not the only cognitive process that selectively activates the occipital cortex of early blind people.
claims.source: Although language is not the only cognitive process that selectively activates the occipital cortex of EB people, it is arguably one of the most puzzling.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous research.

claims.claim: Reorganization of other processes such as auditory motion perception and tactile object recognition appears to follow the topography of the functionally equivalent visual processes in the sighted brain.
claims.source: The reason is that reorganization of other processes, such as auditory motion perception and tactile object recognition, appears to follow the topography of the functionally equivalent visual processes in the sighted brain (Ricciardi et al., 2007a; Amedi et al., 2010; Dormal et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ricciardi et al. (2007a), Amedi et al. (2010), and Dormal et al. (2016).

claims.claim: The hMT+/V5 complex, which is typically involved in visual motion in the sighted, selectively processes auditory motion in blind people.
claims.source: For example, the hMT+/V5 complex, which is typically involved in visual motion in the sighted, selectively processes auditory (Poirier et al., 2006; Dormal et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2016) or tactile (Ricciardi et al., 2007b) motion in blind people.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Poirier et al. (2006), Dormal et al. (2016), and Jiang et al. (2016).

claims.claim: The hMT+/V5 complex, which is typically involved in visual motion in the sighted, selectively processes tactile motion in blind people.
claims.source: For example, the hMT+/V5 complex, which is typically involved in visual motion in the sighted, selectively processes auditory (Poirier et al., 2006; Dormal et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2016) or tactile (Ricciardi et al., 2007b) motion in blind people.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ricciardi et al. (2007b).

claims.claim: The recruitment of occipital cortex for language in blind people is striking in light of the cognitive and evolutionary differences between vision and language.
claims.source: However, in the case of language, such recruitment is striking in light of the cognitive and evolutionary differences between vision and language (Bedny et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bedny et al. (2011).

claims.claim: It has been proposed that at birth, human cortical areas are cognitively pluripotent: capable of assuming a broad range of unrelated cognitive functions.
claims.source: This led to the proposal that, at birth, human cortical areas are cognitively pluripotent: capable of assuming a broad range of unrelated cognitive functions (Bedny, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bedny (2017).

claims.claim: The cognitive pluripotency argument resides on the presupposition that language has no computational relation with vision.
claims.source: However, this argument resides on the presupposition that language has no computational relation with vision.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the assumptions underlying the pluripotency argument.

claims.claim: Rhythmic information in speech has a well-known language-related surrogate in the visual domain: lip movements.
claims.source: But does this proposition tally with what we know about the relationship between the visual system and the classical language network? Rhythmic information in speech has a well-known language-related surrogate in the visual domain: lip movements (Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift, 2012; Park et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift (2012) and Park et al. (2016).

claims.claim: Both acoustic and visual speech signals exhibit rhythmic temporal patterns at prosodic and syllabic rates.
claims.source: Indeed, both acoustic and visual speech signals exhibit rhythmic temporal patterns at prosodic and syllabic rates (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009; Schwartz and Savariaux, 2014; Giordano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chandrasekaran et al. (2009), Schwartz and Savariaux (2014), and Giordano et al. (2017).

claims.claim: The perception of lip kinematics that are naturally linked to amplitude fluctuations in speech serves as an important vehicle for the everyday use of language.
claims.source: The perception of lip kinematics that are naturally linked to amplitude fluctuations in speech serves as an important vehicle for the everyday use of language (Kuhl and Meltzoff, 1982; Weikum et al., 2007; Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift, 2012) and helps language understanding, particularly in noisy conditions (Ross et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kuhl and Meltzoff (1982), Weikum et al. (2007), Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift (2012), and Ross et al. (2007).

claims.claim: Lip reading helps language understanding, particularly in noisy conditions.
claims.source: The perception of lip kinematics that are naturally linked to amplitude fluctuations in speech serves as an important vehicle for the everyday use of language (Kuhl and Meltzoff, 1982; Weikum et al., 2007; Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift, 2012) and helps language understanding, particularly in noisy conditions (Ross et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ross et al. (2007).

claims.claim: Reading lips in the absence of any sound activates both primary and association auditory regions overlapping with regions that are active during the actual perception of spoken words.
claims.source: Indeed, reading lips in the absence of any sound activates both primary and association auditory regions overlapping with regions that are active during the actual perception of spoken words (Calvert et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Calvert et al. (1997).

claims.claim: The synchronicity between auditory and visual speech entrains rhythmic activity in the observer's primary auditory and visual regions.
claims.source: The synchronicity between auditory and visual speech entrains rhythmic activity in the observer's primary auditory and visual regions, and facilitates perception by aligning neural excitability with acoustic or visual speech features (Schroeder et al., 2008; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Mesgarani and Chang, 2012; Peelle and Davis, 2012; van Wassenhove, 2013; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013b; Park et al., 2016; Giordano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The synchronicity between auditory and visual speech facilitates perception by aligning neural excitability with acoustic or visual speech features.
claims.source: The synchronicity between auditory and visual speech entrains rhythmic activity in the observer's primary auditory and visual regions, and facilitates perception by aligning neural excitability with acoustic or visual speech features (Schroeder et al., 2008; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Mesgarani and Chang, 2012; Peelle and Davis, 2012; van Wassenhove, 2013; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013b; Park et al., 2016; Giordano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Both the auditory and the visual components of speech are processed together at the earliest level possible in neural circuitry, based on the shared slow temporal modulations present across modalities.
claims.source: These results strongly suggest that both the auditory and the visual components of speech are processed together at the earliest level possible in neural circuitry, based on the shared slow temporal modulations (around 2–7 Hz range) present across modalities (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chandrasekaran et al. (2009).

claims.claim: Neuronal populations in visual cortex follow the temporal dynamics of lip movements in sighted individuals, similar to the way in which temporal regions follow the acoustic and visual fluctuations of speech.
claims.source: Corroborating this idea, it has been demonstrated that neuronal populations in visual cortex follow the temporal dynamics of lip movements in sighted individuals, similar to the way in which temporal regions follow the acoustic and visual fluctuations of speech (Luo et al., 2010; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013a; Park et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luo et al. (2010), Zion Golumbic et al. (2013a), and Park et al. (2016).

claims.claim: Occipital cortex in the sighted shows enhanced lip tracking when attention is directed to speech content.
claims.source: Similar to temporal cortex, occipital cortex in the sighted also shows enhanced lip tracking when attention is directed to speech content.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous research.

claims.claim: A basic oscillatory architecture for tracking the dynamic aspects of visual-speech in occipital cortex exists even in sighted individuals.
claims.source: This result highlights the fact that a basic oscillatory architecture for tracking the dynamic aspects of (visual-) speech in occipital cortex exists even in sighted individuals.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the evidence of lip tracking in occipital cortex of sighted individuals.

claims.claim: Audiovisual integration of the temporal dynamics of speech has been suggested to play a key role when learning speech early in life.

claims.claim: According to the asymmetric sampling in time model, there is a division of labour between the left- and right auditory cortices.

claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to Elman et al. (1996).

results.result: Behavioral comprehension testing showed that speech intelligibility was significantly reduced in the 1-channel vocoded condition but not in the 8-channel condition, with no differences between early blind and sighted groups in comprehension performance across conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C25 collectively demonstrate successful behavioral manipulation of intelligibility through vocoding. Statistical analyses using linear mixed-effects models show significant effects of intelligibility (p<0.001) but no effects of blindness or interaction, with orthogonal contrasts confirming that natural and 8-channel conditions were equally intelligible while 1-channel was at chance. The behavioral data validate the experimental manipulation and control for group differences in attention or motivation.

results.result: MEG coherence analysis revealed maximal cerebro-acoustic coherence between 6-7 Hz over temporal sensors, with source reconstruction confirming strongest coherence in bilateral temporal lobes including primary auditory cortex across both groups and all conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 establish the basic neural tracking of speech envelope at syllabic rate. The peak frequency (6-7 Hz) is appropriately attributed to Italian syllabic rate (~7 Hz) versus English (~6.2 Hz) used in prior studies. Source reconstruction confirms expected temporal lobe localization. These findings replicate established speech tracking phenomena and provide the foundation for subsequent group comparisons.

results.result: Right superior and middle temporal cortex showed stronger synchronization to intelligible versus unintelligible speech across both groups, suggesting this region interfaces acoustic speech processing and comprehension.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 demonstrate intelligibility modulation of speech tracking in right STG/MTG (p<0.05, FWE-corrected). The finding is appropriately interpreted as an interface between perception and comprehension. The result is consistent with the asymmetric sampling in time model and replicates prior findings. Statistical correction and bilateral group analysis support the conclusion.

results.result: Early blind individuals showed enhanced cerebro-acoustic coherence in parieto-occipital cortex (centered on bilateral Precuneus) compared to sighted individuals, irrespective of speech intelligibility, suggesting involvement in low-level acoustic processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35, C63, C67 establish enhanced speech envelope tracking in parieto-occipital regions of early blind participants (p<0.05, FWE-corrected). The lack of intelligibility modulation appropriately supports interpretation as low-level acoustic processing. The finding is consistent with prior work showing general auditory responses in this region after early visual deprivation (C64-C66). The statistical approach and interpretation are sound.

results.result: Right calcarine sulcus (primary visual cortex) in early blind individuals showed selectively enhanced synchronization to intelligible speech compared to sighted individuals, with no overall group difference across conditions, indicating sensitivity to speech intelligibility rather than simple acoustic features.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C45 demonstrate a critical interaction effect: calcarine sulcus responds more to intelligible speech in early blind versus sighted (p<0.05, FWE-corrected in ROI; p<0.005 uncorrected whole-brain). Post-hoc tests confirm the effect is driven by intelligible conditions (p=0.004) not unintelligible (p=0.29). The lack of difference between natural and 8-channel conditions (C39-C40) appropriately rules out low-level acoustic degradation as the driver. The absence of main effect of group (C43-C44) strengthens the interpretation that this reflects intelligibility-specific processing rather than general auditory enhancement.

results.result: Early blind individuals showed enhanced functional connectivity (phase-locking value) between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus compared to sighted individuals, with no modulation by intelligibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54, C68, C130 demonstrate increased connectivity between occipital and temporal regions in early blind (χ²[1]=4.32, p=0.038) using phase-locking value analysis in the theta range. Linear mixed-effects models appropriately control for repeated measures. The lack of intelligibility effects (p=0.241) and interaction (p=0.716) is clearly reported. The analysis is restricted to functionally-defined ROIs from prior analyses, which is methodologically sound though limits generalizability.

results.result: Directional connectivity analysis revealed that sighted individuals show feed-forward projections from calcarine sulcus to superior temporal gyrus, while early blind individuals show a more balanced connectivity profile trending toward the reverse direction.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C62, C131 demonstrate altered directionality using phase-slope index (χ²[1]=4.54, p=0.033). Post-hoc one-sample t-tests show significant CS→STG bias in sighted (t[14]=-2.22, p=0.044) but not blind (t[16]=0.74, p=0.47). The statistical approach is appropriate for directional connectivity. However, the 'trend' toward reverse direction in blind is not statistically significant, so the interpretation should be more cautious. The finding supports a reverse hierarchical model but the directionality in blind remains uncertain.

results.result: The occipital cortex of early blind individuals adopts an architecture that tracks speech material at both acoustic (parieto-occipital) and intelligibility-sensitive (calcarine) levels, with enhanced and altered connectivity to temporal regions, suggesting the occipital cortex does not fully abstract from reorganized sensory inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C6 synthesize the major findings into a coherent interpretation. The conclusion that occipital cortex tracks speech material is directly supported by the coherence data (C33-C45). The claim about not fully abstracting from sensory inputs (C6) is appropriately supported by the finding of acoustic-level tracking in parieto-occipital regions (C33-C35) and intelligibility-sensitive tracking in calcarine (C36-C45). The connectivity findings (C4-C5, C52-C62) provide mechanistic support. This represents the primary conclusion of the manuscript.

results.result: The authors propose that reorganization in blind occipital cortex may be constrained by pre-existing audiovisual speech integration pathways present in sighted individuals (biased connectivity hypothesis), with the mapping of language onto occipital cortex building upon oscillatory architecture typically linking auditory and visual speech rhythm.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111, C124-C127, C164 present a mechanistic hypothesis supported by extensive citations to prior work on audiovisual speech integration (C88-C106) and biased connectivity (C107-C109). While the hypothesis is plausible and well-motivated by the literature, it remains speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION for most claims). The current data show enhanced connectivity and altered directionality but do not directly test whether this arises from pre-existing audiovisual pathways versus other mechanisms. The hypothesis generates testable predictions but requires additional experiments (e.g., developmental studies, direct manipulation of connectivity) for validation.

results.result: The findings contrast with previous proposals that occipital involvement in speech processing is abstracted from sensory input and purely reflects higher-level operations, instead demonstrating that occipital regions respond to speech at a sensory level.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116, C119, C161 present an important theoretical contrast with prior work (C112-C113). The demonstration that peri-calcarine cortex aligns to temporal dynamics of intelligible speech (C115) and is functionally connected to auditory regions (C116) directly supports this interpretation. The finding of acoustic-level tracking in parieto-occipital regions (C33-C35) further supports sensory-level processing. However, the interpretation could be more nuanced: the intelligibility sensitivity in calcarine (C36-C45) suggests some level of abstraction beyond pure sensory processing. The contrast is valid but the dichotomy between 'sensory' and 'abstract' may be oversimplified.

results.result: The study replicates previous findings of enhanced phase coupling between right hemisphere and speech envelope at syllabic rate, with right hemispheric sensitivity to intelligible speech observed in both temporal and occipital regions of blind individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C139 appropriately situate the findings within the asymmetric sampling in time model (C133-C137). The right hemisphere lateralization of intelligibility effects in both STG (C31) and calcarine (C36-C38) is clearly demonstrated. The replication of prior speech tracking findings (C138) strengthens confidence in the methods. The observation of coinciding right hemisphere effects (C139) is interesting but the functional significance of this lateralization pattern requires further investigation.

results.result: The behavioral task did not allow direct assessment of the link between reorganized occipital cortex and speech comprehension performance, as performance was at ceiling for intelligible conditions and at chance for unintelligible conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149, C159 appropriately acknowledge a key limitation. The ceiling/floor effects in behavioral performance (Table 1) preclude correlating brain activity with individual differences in comprehension. The authors appropriately discuss the complexity of linking single-region activity to behavior (C148-C149) and cite relevant work on redeployment mechanisms (C150-C158). This limitation is important for interpreting the functional significance of the findings, though it does not invalidate the neural observations.

results.result: The study included 17 early blind and 16 sighted participants matched for age, with blind participants being congenitally blind or severely visually impaired from birth, all proficient Braille readers and native Italian speakers.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C173 describe the participant sample. Age matching is confirmed statistically (C169: t[30]=0.19, p=0.85). The description of visual status (C170) is appropriate though includes some heterogeneity (residual vision before age 3-4 in some participants, one participant with sight loss at age 10). This heterogeneity could affect results but is typical of early blind samples. Exclusion criteria (C172-C173) are appropriate. Sample size (n=17 EB, n=16 SI) is reasonable for MEG studies but relatively small for detecting subtle effects.

results.result: The experimental design used natural speech and two vocoded conditions (8-channel maintaining intelligibility, 1-channel removing intelligibility) from Italian audiobooks, with MEG recorded at 1 kHz from a 306-sensor system.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C178 describe the experimental methods. The vocoding manipulation is well-established and appropriately implemented. The perceptual characteristics (C176-C177) are validated by behavioral data (C19-C24). MEG acquisition parameters (C178) are standard. The use of Italian stimuli is appropriate for the participant population and explains the 6-7 Hz peak frequency (C27-C28). The naturalistic audiobook stimuli enhance ecological validity compared to synthetic speech.

results.result: The study supports the view that functional specialization in human cortex results from dynamic interplay between genetic and environmental factors during development rather than being predetermined at birth.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C166 present the broad theoretical implication. The demonstration of language-related reorganization in occipital cortex following early visual deprivation provides evidence for experience-dependent plasticity. However, the interpretation that this argues against predetermined organization may be too strong. The findings are equally consistent with constrained plasticity (biased connectivity hypothesis, C107-C111) where reorganization follows pre-existing pathways. The data support plasticity but do not definitively resolve the nature-nurture debate about cortical organization.
